items.meaning: To add another negative event or problem to an already difficult situation.
items.example: Then, to make matters worse, my car broke down on the way to the airport.
items.plain: Then, another bad thing happened: my car broke down on the way to the airport.
items.note: Used when recounting a series of unfortunate events, often with a slightly dramatic tone.

items.meaning: Used to introduce information that was discovered later, often unexpectedly.
items.example: I thought I'd lost my keys, but as it turned out, they were in my other bag.
items.plain: I thought I'd lost my keys, but I later discovered they were in my other bag.
items.note: Common in storytelling to reveal a surprising or clarifying piece of information.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that is surprising or hard to believe.
items.example: Believe it or not, I ran into our old professor at the grocery store yesterday.
items.plain: It's surprising, but I ran into our old professor at the grocery store yesterday.
items.note: Adds emphasis to an unexpected event, inviting the listener's surprise.

items.meaning: Used to describe a sudden, unexpected event that happened immediately after something else.
items.example: I was just standing there, and the next thing I knew, the alarm went off.
items.plain: I was just standing there, and suddenly, the alarm went off.
items.note: Conveys a sense of speed and surprise, often used to build tension in a story.

items.meaning: Used to introduce the beginning of a story or a sequence of events.
items.example: It all started when I decided to take that last-minute trip to Rome.
items.plain: The story began when I decided to take that last-minute trip to Rome.
items.note: A classic opening for an anecdote, setting the scene for what's to come.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize the lasting impact or vivid memory of an event.
items.example: I'll never forget the look on his face when he realized his mistake.
items.plain: I will always remember the look on his face when he realized his mistake.
items.note: Highlights a particularly memorable moment, often emotional or significant.

items.meaning: Used to grab the listener's attention and indicate a surprising story is coming.
items.example: You won't believe what happened to me on my commute this morning!
items.plain: I have a surprising story about what happened to me on my commute this morning!
items.note: An informal and engaging way to start a story, creating immediate interest.

items.text: to cut a long story short
items.form: to cut a long story short
items.meaning: To summarize a lengthy explanation or narrative quickly.
items.example: Anyway, to cut a long story short, we ended up missing our flight.
items.plain: Anyway, we ended up missing our flight because I'm summarizing.
items.note: Signals that you are skipping details and getting to the main point. Slightly formal.

items.meaning: A more informal way to summarize a lengthy explanation or narrative quickly.
items.example: Long story short, the project was a huge success despite the initial problems.
items.plain: To summarize, the project was a huge success despite the initial problems.
items.note: A very common, informal way to get to the point quickly. Often used mid-story.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a frank or sincere opinion, often one that might be surprising.
items.example: To be honest, I wasn't expecting the presentation to go so well.
items.plain: Frankly, I wasn't expecting the presentation to go so well.
items.note: Adds a personal, sincere touch to a statement, often revealing a true feeling.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a surprising or coincidental piece of information.
items.example: Strangely enough, I was just thinking about that exact topic yesterday.
items.plain: It's a coincidence, but I was just thinking about that exact topic yesterday.
items.note: Highlights an unexpected connection or occurrence, often used in casual conversation.

items.meaning: Used to reveal information that was discovered or became known later.
items.example: We thought he was busy, but it turns out that he was just on vacation.
items.plain: We thought he was busy, but we discovered he was just on vacation.
items.note: Commonly used to explain a previous misunderstanding or reveal a fact.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize the most important idea or message being conveyed.
items.example: The point is, we need to learn from our mistakes and move forward.
items.plain: The most important thing is that we need to learn from our mistakes and move forward.
items.note: Directs attention to the core message or conclusion of a discussion or story.

items.meaning: Used to introduce an explanation of a past event or situation.
items.example: What happened was, the train was delayed, so I missed my connection.
items.plain: The train was delayed, so I missed my connection.
items.note: A common way to begin explaining a sequence of events or a problem.

items.meaning: Used to share a specific thought or internal reaction from a past moment.
items.example: I remember thinking, 'This is going to be a disaster,' right before it started.
items.plain: I thought, 'This is going to be a disaster,' right before it started.
items.note: Adds a personal, reflective layer to storytelling, revealing inner thoughts.

items.meaning: Used to express extreme surprise or astonishment at something seen.
items.example: When I opened the door, I couldn't believe my eyes; the whole room was decorated!
items.plain: When I opened the door, I was extremely surprised; the whole room was decorated!
items.note: A strong expression of visual surprise, often used for dramatic effect.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that something unexpected happened, causing surprise.
items.example: I asked for a refund, and to my surprise, they gave me one immediately.
items.plain: I asked for a refund, and unexpectedly, they gave me one immediately.
items.note: A common way to introduce an unexpected positive or negative outcome.

items.meaning: Used to describe something happening very quickly and unexpectedly.
items.example: We were talking quietly, and all of a sudden, the lights went out.
items.plain: We were talking quietly, and suddenly, the lights went out.
items.note: Similar to 'out of nowhere,' but often refers to a change in state or action.

items.meaning: Used to describe something happening very quickly, without conscious awareness.
items.example: I started working on the report, and before I knew it, hours had passed.
items.plain: I started working on the report, and hours passed very quickly.
items.note: Conveys a sense of time passing rapidly or an event unfolding quickly.

items.meaning: Used to describe suddenly realizing or understanding something.
items.example: After a few minutes, it dawned on me that I had left my phone at home.
items.plain: After a few minutes, I suddenly realized that I had left my phone at home.
items.note: Refers to a moment of sudden insight or realization, often after some thought.

items.meaning: Used to express complete lack of prior knowledge or awareness about something.
items.example: I had no idea she was planning to move abroad until she told me last week.
items.plain: I didn't know she was planning to move abroad until she told me last week.
items.note: Expresses genuine surprise or ignorance about a fact or situation.

items.meaning: Used to describe an event or piece of news that was extremely surprising and unexpected.
items.example: When they announced the merger, it was a complete shock to everyone in the office.
items.plain: When they announced the merger, it was extremely surprising to everyone in the office.
items.note: Emphasizes the intensity of the surprise, often for significant news.

items.meaning: Used to express great surprise, often mixed with wonder or disbelief.
items.example: To my astonishment, the package arrived a week earlier than expected.
items.plain: I was very surprised when the package arrived a week earlier than expected.
items.note: A slightly more formal way to express strong surprise, similar to 'to my surprise'.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize that one remembers something very clearly and precisely.
items.example: I distinctly remember locking the door, so I don't know how it's open now.
items.plain: I clearly remember locking the door, so I don't know how it's open now.
items.note: Adds credibility to a memory, often used when there's a discrepancy.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a surprising or ironic detail in a story.
items.example: The funny thing is, I almost didn't go to that party, and it was amazing.
items.plain: It's ironic that I almost didn't go to that party, and it was amazing.
items.note: Highlights an unexpected or amusing aspect of a situation.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a particularly unbelievable or absurd detail in a story.
items.example: The crazy thing is, he actually managed to finish the marathon with a broken shoe.
items.plain: It's unbelievable that he managed to finish the marathon with a broken shoe.
items.note: Emphasizes the extraordinary or unbelievable nature of an event.

items.meaning: Used to describe an action that was on the verge of happening but was interrupted.
items.example: I was about to leave when my phone rang with important news.
items.plain: I was just going to leave when my phone rang with important news.
items.note: Creates a sense of anticipation, often leading to a turning point in a story.

items.meaning: Used to describe an event that happened at the exact moment another action was taking place.
items.example: Just as I was falling asleep, I heard a loud noise outside.
items.plain: At the exact moment I was falling asleep, I heard a loud noise outside.
items.note: Connects two simultaneous events, often one interrupting the other.

items.meaning: Used to describe a subjective experience or sensation, often using a comparison.
items.example: When I finally finished the project, it felt like a huge weight had been lifted.
items.plain: When I finally finished the project, I felt a huge sense of relief.
items.note: Helps convey emotions or physical sensations to the listener.

items.meaning: Used to express a premonition or intuition about something that later proved true.
items.example: I had a feeling the meeting would be cancelled, and sure enough, it was.
items.plain: I had an intuition the meeting would be cancelled, and it was.
items.note: Suggests a sense of foresight or intuition, often used after an event.

items.meaning: Used to describe an action or feeling that was irresistible or unavoidable.
items.example: When she told that joke, I couldn't help but laugh out loud.
items.plain: When she told that joke, I had to laugh out loud.
items.note: Indicates an involuntary reaction or a strong urge to do something.

items.meaning: Used to describe a situation where a bad outcome was narrowly avoided.
items.example: The car swerved just in time; it was a close call, we almost crashed.
items.plain: The car swerved just in time; we almost crashed, but avoided it.
items.note: Emphasizes the danger and the narrow escape from a negative situation.

items.meaning: Used to highlight a particular detail or aspect that made a strong impression.
items.example: What struck me was how calm she remained throughout the entire crisis.
items.plain: I was particularly impressed by how calm she remained throughout the entire crisis.
items.note: Draws attention to a specific, impactful observation or realization.

items.meaning: Used to express being surprised or shocked, often in a negative way.
items.example: I was taken aback by his sudden outburst during the presentation.
items.plain: I was surprised by his sudden outburst during the presentation.
items.note: Indicates a moment of shock or surprise that causes a pause or hesitation.

items.meaning: Used to state something that is so obvious it doesn't need to be said.
items.example: It goes without saying that we need to prioritize safety in this project.
items.plain: It's obvious that we need to prioritize safety in this project.
items.note: Often used to reinforce a widely accepted truth or a fundamental principle.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a mitigating factor or a balanced perspective in a discussion.
items.example: He made a mistake, but to be fair, he was under a lot of pressure.
items.plain: He made a mistake, but he was under a lot of pressure, which explains it.
items.note: Offers a more balanced view, acknowledging another side of an argument.

items.meaning: Used to offer an opinion or piece of information that may or may not be helpful.
items.example: For what it's worth, I think you did a great job despite the challenges.
items.plain: I think you did a great job despite the challenges, though my opinion might not matter much.
items.note: A humble way to offer advice or an opinion, acknowledging its subjective value.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that one will provide a short, concise explanation or story.
items.example: I'll keep it brief, but I wanted to share a quick update on the project.
items.plain: I will be quick, but I wanted to share a quick update on the project.
items.note: A polite way to signal that you won't take up much of the listener's time.

items.text: the moral of the story is
items.form: The moral of the story is
items.meaning: Used to state the lesson or main takeaway from an anecdote or experience.
items.example: The moral of the story is, always double-check your travel documents.
items.plain: The lesson from this experience is, always double-check your travel documents.
items.note: A classic way to conclude a story by explicitly stating its lesson.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a conclusion or general truth illustrated by a specific event.
items.example: He worked hard and got the promotion; it just goes to show that effort pays off.
items.plain: He worked hard and got the promotion; this proves that effort pays off.
items.note: Connects a specific event to a broader principle or observation.

items.meaning: Used to express that one gains wisdom or knowledge from past mistakes or experiences.
items.example: I forgot to back up my files, and lost everything. Well, you live and learn.
items.plain: I forgot to back up my files, and lost everything. I learned from that mistake.
items.note: A common, slightly resigned way to acknowledge a lesson learned from experience.

items.meaning: Used to express appreciation for a funny story, joke, or clever remark.
items.example: He told a story about his dog chasing a squirrel, and I thought, 'That's a good one!'
items.plain: He told a story about his dog chasing a squirrel, and I thought it was funny.
items.note: A casual and positive reaction to someone else's anecdote or joke.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a related story or memory triggered by the current conversation.
items.example: That reminds me of the time I accidentally locked myself out of my apartment.
items.plain: That makes me think of the time I accidentally locked myself out of my apartment.
items.note: A natural way to transition from one story to another in conversation.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a related topic that was just mentioned or implied.
items.example: We're talking about travel; speaking of which, have you booked your flight yet?
items.plain: We're talking about travel; by the way, have you booked your flight yet?
items.note: A common conversational connector to bring up a relevant point.

items.meaning: Used to introduce one side of an argument or a particular perspective.
items.example: On the one hand, the new policy is more efficient, but it also has drawbacks.
items.plain: One perspective is that the new policy is more efficient, but it also has drawbacks.
items.note: Often followed by 'on the other hand' to present a balanced view.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a contrasting argument or an alternative perspective.
items.example: On the one hand, it's expensive, but on the other hand, it's very durable.
items.plain: It's expensive, but alternatively, it's very durable.
items.note: Used to present a contrasting point, usually after 'on the one hand'.

items.meaning: Used to summarize something very briefly and concisely.
items.example: So, in a nutshell, we need to redesign the entire marketing strategy.
items.plain: So, to summarize briefly, we need to redesign the entire marketing strategy.
items.note: An informal way to give a quick summary, often at the end of an explanation.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that a statement is an understatement, implying something more extreme.
items.example: The meeting was challenging, to put it mildly; it was a complete disaster.
items.plain: The meeting was challenging, but that's an understatement; it was a complete disaster.
items.note: Emphasizes that the speaker is being polite or restrained in their description.

items.meaning: Used to clarify or rephrase a previous statement, or to emphasize a point.
items.example: It's not ideal, I mean to say, we could do much better with more resources.
items.plain: It's not ideal; I want to clarify that we could do much better with more resources.
items.note: A common filler phrase used to elaborate or correct oneself.

items.meaning: Used to introduce one's personal opinion or perspective on a matter.
items.example: The way I see it, we should focus on long-term solutions, not quick fixes.
items.plain: In my opinion, we should focus on long-term solutions, not quick fixes.
items.note: A polite and common way to offer a personal viewpoint in a discussion.

items.meaning: Used to clarify a situation by stating what is not the main reason or issue.
items.example: It's not so much that I dislike the idea, but I'm concerned about the cost.
items.plain: The main reason isn't that I dislike the idea, but I'm concerned about the cost.
items.note: Helps to refine an explanation, distinguishing between primary and secondary reasons.

items.meaning: Used to clarify the main point or intention behind one's words.
items.example: I know it sounds complicated, but what I'm getting at is we need a new strategy.
items.plain: I know it sounds complicated, but my main point is we need a new strategy.
items.note: Used when trying to make a complex point clear or to summarize one's argument.

items.meaning: Used to express uncertainty or hesitation about a fact or possibility.
items.example: I'm not sure if I mentioned this before, but I'm moving next month.
items.plain: I don't know if I mentioned this before, but I'm moving next month.
items.note: A polite way to introduce potentially new information or express doubt.

items.meaning: Used when struggling to articulate a thought or to clarify a complex idea.
items.example: It's difficult to explain, but I'm trying to say that we need more flexibility.
items.plain: It's difficult to explain, but I mean that we need more flexibility.
items.note: Indicates an effort to communicate a nuanced or challenging concept.

items.meaning: Used when attempting to clarify a situation or concept for someone.
items.example: I know it sounds strange, but I'm trying to explain why I made that decision.
items.plain: I know it sounds strange, but I want to clarify why I made that decision.
items.note: Often used when the listener seems confused or needs more context.

items.text: I'm trying to make sense of
items.form: I'm trying to make sense of
items.meaning: Used to describe an attempt to understand a confusing or illogical situation.
items.example: I'm trying to make sense of why they changed the schedule without telling anyone.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand why they changed the schedule without telling anyone.
items.note: Expresses a process of mental effort to comprehend something perplexing.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that a concept or situation is difficult to articulate clearly.
items.example: It's hard to explain, but I just had a bad feeling about the whole thing.
items.plain: It's difficult to articulate, but I just had a bad feeling about the whole thing.
items.note: Often used when describing an intuition or a complex emotional state.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that a visual, sensory, or abstract experience is difficult to put into words.
items.example: The view from the mountain was incredible; it's hard to describe how beautiful it was.
items.plain: The view from the mountain was incredible; it's difficult to put into words how beautiful it was.
items.note: Commonly used for subjective experiences like beauty, taste, or feelings.

items.text: I can't quite put my finger on it
items.form: I can't quite put my finger on it
items.meaning: Used to express that one knows something is wrong or unusual but can't identify exactly what.
items.example: Something feels off about this proposal, but I can't quite put my finger on it.
items.plain: Something feels wrong about this proposal, but I can't identify the exact problem.
items.note: Indicates a vague sense of unease or an inability to pinpoint a specific issue.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a comparison or analogy to help explain something.
items.example: Learning a new language, it's a bit like building a house from scratch.
items.plain: Learning a new language is similar to building a house from scratch.
items.note: A common way to make an abstract concept more understandable through comparison.

items.meaning: A more informal way to introduce a comparison or analogy to help explain something.
items.example: This new software, it's kind of like a simplified version of the old one.
items.plain: This new software is similar to a simplified version of the old one.
items.note: Very common in casual conversation to offer a quick, informal comparison.

items.meaning: Used to offer a tentative or slightly hesitant opinion or description.
items.example: I suppose you could say the meeting was productive, though we didn't decide much.
items.plain: You could perhaps say the meeting was productive, though we didn't decide much.
items.note: Suggests a cautious or qualified agreement, or a less definitive statement.

items.meaning: A more informal way to offer a tentative or slightly hesitant opinion or description.
items.example: I guess you could say I'm happy with the results, but there's room for improvement.
items.plain: I suppose I'm happy with the results, but there's room for improvement.
items.note: Similar to 'I suppose you could say,' but more common in everyday speech.

items.text: if you know what I mean
items.form: if you know what I mean
items.meaning: Used to check if the listener understands an implied meaning or subtle point.
items.example: The atmosphere was a bit tense, if you know what I mean, after the announcement.
items.plain: The atmosphere was a bit tense, and I hope you understand the subtle implication.
items.note: Often used when hinting at something or referring to shared unspoken knowledge.

items.meaning: Used to express that a situation is common or understandable, appealing to shared experience.
items.example: Sometimes you just need a quiet evening at home, you know how it is.
items.plain: Sometimes you just need a quiet evening at home, as that's a common feeling.
items.note: Creates a sense of camaraderie, implying the listener shares the same experience.

items.meaning: Used to describe a situation that is unavoidable, inexplicable, or simply part of life.
items.example: The flight was delayed again. Oh well, it's one of those things, I guess.
items.plain: The flight was delayed again. Oh well, it's an unavoidable part of life, I guess.
items.note: A resigned way to accept a common or frustrating situation.

items.meaning: Used to state that something happens frequently or is not unusual.
items.example: Losing your luggage on a long trip, unfortunately, it's a common occurrence.
items.plain: Losing your luggage on a long trip, unfortunately, happens frequently.
items.note: Describes something as a regular or expected event, often with a neutral tone.

items.meaning: Used to state that something happens infrequently or is unusual.
items.example: Getting everyone together for dinner these days, it's a rare occasion.
items.plain: Getting everyone together for dinner these days, it happens infrequently.
items.note: Highlights the infrequency or special nature of an event.

items.meaning: Used to express that something is inevitable and will happen eventually.
items.example: With all the changes, it's a matter of time before the company restructures.
items.plain: With all the changes, it's inevitable that the company will restructure eventually.
items.note: Suggests certainty about a future event, often with a sense of anticipation.

items.meaning: Used to state that something is subjective and open to different viewpoints.
items.example: Whether that design is good or bad, it's a matter of opinion, really.
items.plain: Whether that design is good or bad, it's subjective, really.
items.note: Emphasizes that there is no single correct answer or universal agreement.

items.meaning: Used to state that something is objectively true and not open to debate.
items.example: The earth is round; it's a matter of fact, not a belief.
items.plain: The earth is round; it's objectively true, not a belief.
items.note: Contrasts with 'matter of opinion,' asserting objective truth.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge that someone has made a valid and relevant observation.
items.example: You're right, we haven't considered the budget. That's a good point.
items.plain: You're right, we haven't considered the budget. That's a valid observation.
items.note: A common way to agree with or acknowledge the value of someone's contribution.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge that someone has made a reasonable and justifiable observation.
items.example: I hadn't thought of it that way. That's a fair point about the timeline.
items.plain: I hadn't thought of it that way. That's a reasonable observation about the timeline.
items.note: Similar to 'good point,' but often implies a concession or understanding.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge that someone has made a logically sound and well-reasoned observation.
items.example: You're right, the data does support that conclusion. That's a valid point.
items.plain: You're right, the data does support that conclusion. That's a logically sound observation.
items.note: Emphasizes the logical strength and correctness of an argument.

items.meaning: Used to indicate understanding of someone's argument or perspective.
items.example: I see your point about the risks, but I still think we should proceed.
items.plain: I understand your argument about the risks, but I still think we should proceed.
items.note: Expresses comprehension, not necessarily agreement. Can be a polite disagreement.

items.meaning: A more informal way to indicate understanding of someone's argument or perspective.
items.example: Okay, I get your point; we need to prioritize the urgent tasks first.
items.plain: Okay, I understand your argument; we need to prioritize the urgent tasks first.
items.note: Common in casual conversation, similar to 'I see your point'.

items.meaning: Used to express that something is logical, reasonable, or understandable.
items.example: Ah, so that's why the system crashed. That makes sense now.
items.plain: Ah, so that's why the system crashed. That is logical now.
items.note: A common and versatile phrase for acknowledging understanding or agreement.

items.meaning: Used to express empathy or acknowledge that a feeling or action is reasonable.
items.example: You're tired after that long flight? That's understandable.
items.plain: You're tired after that long flight? That is reasonable.
items.note: Shows empathy and acknowledges the validity of someone's feelings or situation.

items.meaning: Used to describe a moment when a significant change or shift in direction occurred.
items.example: Meeting her in college, it was a turning point in my life and career.
items.plain: Meeting her in college was a moment of significant change in my life and career.
items.note: Highlights a pivotal moment that altered the course of events.

items.meaning: Used to summarize the main points of a discussion or story quickly.
items.example: To recap briefly, we've decided to postpone the launch until next quarter.
items.plain: To summarize quickly, we've decided to postpone the launch until next quarter.
items.note: Often used in formal or semi-formal settings to review information.

items.meaning: Used to introduce positive news or a successful outcome.
items.example: I'm happy to report that the fundraising event exceeded all our expectations.
items.plain: I'm pleased to announce that the fundraising event exceeded all our expectations.
items.note: A formal or semi-formal way to deliver good news, often in a professional context.

items.meaning: Used to introduce bad news or an unwelcome piece of information politely.
items.example: I'm afraid to say that we've run into some unexpected technical difficulties.
items.plain: I regret to inform you that we've run into some unexpected technical difficulties.
items.note: A polite and common way to deliver negative news, softening the impact.

items.meaning: Used to draw attention to an important or relevant piece of information.
items.example: It's worth noting that the initial budget was much smaller than the final one.
items.plain: It's important to note that the initial budget was much smaller than the final one.
items.note: Highlights a detail that adds context or significance to the discussion.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that is obvious or expected, but still worth mentioning.
items.example: Needless to say, after working all night, I was completely exhausted.
items.plain: It's obvious that after working all night, I was completely exhausted.
items.note: Emphasizes the obviousness of a consequence or fact.

items.meaning: A stronger version of 'to be honest,' emphasizing complete frankness.
items.example: To be perfectly honest, I think the new design is a step backward.
items.plain: Frankly, I think the new design is a step backward.
items.note: Used when expressing a strong, unreserved opinion, often critical.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge a fact or feeling, often one that is slightly surprising or reluctant.
items.example: I must admit, I was quite nervous before my job interview.
items.plain: I have to confess, I was quite nervous before my job interview.
items.note: Adds a personal touch, revealing a candid thought or feeling.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that is so obvious it doesn't need to be said.
items.example: It goes without saying that teamwork is essential for this project's success.
items.plain: It's obvious that teamwork is essential for this project's success.
items.note: A slightly more formal version of 'it goes without saying'.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize the truth or certainty of a statement, often based on experience.
items.example: It was a tough negotiation, I can tell you, but we got a good deal.
items.plain: It was a tough negotiation, I assure you, but we got a good deal.
items.note: Adds conviction and personal experience to a statement.

items.meaning: Used to state the most important fact or the essential conclusion of a matter.
items.example: We can discuss details, but the bottom line is, we need to increase sales.
items.plain: We can discuss details, but the most important fact is, we need to increase sales.
items.note: A common business idiom, used to get to the core issue or final decision.

items.meaning: Used to add a more exact or specific detail to a previous statement.
items.example: The meeting starts at 10:00 AM, to be precise, in Conference Room B.
items.plain: The meeting starts at 10:00 AM, specifically, in Conference Room B.
items.note: Adds accuracy and clarity, often used for factual information.

items.meaning: Used to offer an opinion or observation without intending to argue or insist.
items.example: I'm just saying, maybe we should consider other options before deciding.
items.plain: I'm simply suggesting that maybe we should consider other options before deciding.
items.note: A casual way to express a thought, often to soften a suggestion or criticism.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that is generally accepted as true or reasonable.
items.example: It's fair to say that the project faced numerous unexpected challenges.
items.plain: It's reasonable to state that the project faced numerous unexpected challenges.
items.note: Suggests a consensus or a widely acknowledged truth, often diplomatic.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize the truth or reliability of a statement, often to alleviate doubt.
items.example: I can assure you, the data has been thoroughly checked and is accurate.
items.plain: I promise you, the data has been thoroughly checked and is accurate.
items.note: Conveys confidence and aims to convince the listener of a fact.

items.meaning: Used to express that something is not surprising, given the circumstances.
items.example: He worked 70 hours a week; it's no wonder he's feeling burnt out.
items.plain: He worked 70 hours a week; it's not surprising he's feeling burnt out.
items.note: Connects a cause to an expected effect, often with a sense of inevitability.

items.meaning: Used to provide a precise detail or correction to a previous statement.
items.example: The meeting is at 3 PM, to be exact, not 3:30.
items.plain: The meeting is at 3 PM, precisely, not 3:30.
items.note: Similar to 'to be precise,' used for factual accuracy.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize a statement, often to convince or impress the listener.
items.example: That concert was incredible, I'm telling you, the best I've ever seen!
items.plain: That concert was incredible, I assure you, the best I've ever seen!
items.note: Adds force and conviction to an opinion or description.

items.meaning: Used to state that something is an accepted fact or a fundamental assumption.
items.example: It's a given that we'll need to work extra hours to meet the deadline.
items.plain: It's an accepted fact that we'll need to work extra hours to meet the deadline.
items.note: Implies that a point is so obvious or fundamental it doesn't need discussion.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that a previous statement was a joke and not meant seriously.
items.example: I'm going to quit and move to a desert island. I'm just kidding, of course!
items.plain: I'm going to quit and move to a desert island. I'm joking, of course!
items.note: A common phrase to lighten the mood after a sarcastic or exaggerated remark.

items.meaning: Used to express regret or disappointment about a situation.
items.example: It's a shame that the event was cancelled due to bad weather.
items.plain: It's disappointing that the event was cancelled due to bad weather.
items.note: Conveys a sense of regret for an unfortunate or missed opportunity.

items.meaning: Used to express regret or sadness about a situation.
items.example: It's a pity that we couldn't spend more time together on your visit.
items.plain: It's regrettable that we couldn't spend more time together on your visit.
items.note: Similar to 'it's a shame that,' expressing mild regret or sorrow.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a frank or honest statement, often one that might be surprising or negative.
items.example: I'm not going to lie, the presentation was a bit boring.
items.plain: To be honest, the presentation was a bit boring.
items.note: An informal way to signal complete honesty, even if the truth is uncomfortable.

i guess you could say.note: Checker slip: The phrase is used to introduce a tentative or qualified statement about one's feelings.

the bottom line is.note: Checker slip: The key accurately captures the meaning of the expression as used in the example.
